story_text.value:
I've been working on a game Hello Triangle for a while. In the game, you build a GPU one part at a time by wiring circuits, and renders a picture on the screen with what your circuit computes. I have a free demo available that goes up to drawing a triangle, while I'm still working on the rest of the game.

You don't start from logic gates. The game starts with adders and comparators. Every wire just carries a fixed point number, and there are no bit widths to think about. The reason of using fixed point numbers is that veteran players of Turing Complete can skip the bits part they already player, while players who are new to programming can still jump right in.

The circuit simulator is written in Go and the game UI is written in Godot, and they communitate through stdio. I also built a score server that players can upload their scores and compare with each other through score histograms.

The demo is available on Steam (Windows/macOS/Linux), there's also an itch.io build if you don't use Steam. Curious what you think, and where you get stuck!

title.value: Show HN: Hello Triangle, a puzzle game where you build a GPU

story_text.value:
Most chess apps try to replicate the classic 64-square experience. Over the last few years, I’ve been doing the opposite—breaking chess down into fast, bite-sized mobile games on smaller boards, each designed to isolate and gamify a single skill:

Firstchess: Bite-sized lessons to learn the fundamentals on a compact board.

Halfchess: Focused purely on endgame thinking on a smaller grid.

Phantom Chess: Blind/memory-based chess on a mini board.

Schmess: Real-time speed chess where multiple pieces move simultaneously.

You can try all four live apps at https://halfchess.com.

I plan to build more chess/poker mini games if I can figure out a distribution for these. If you know any media outlets or micro influencers who can cover my games, do let me know.

title.value: Show HN: Four bite-sized chess puzzle games built on micro-boards

story_text.value:
Most of the alternatives diverged from the true fun of MSPaint that I had as a child. My children also seem to enjoy this. The closest existing project was "Drawing" on Linux, but I felt it couldn't decide if it was a vector or a raster editor, and this confused my kids, and made good fill pours difficult.

Features added beyond original Paint:

- Draw circles starting from the center.

- OKLCH Palette

- Visible pixel grid when zoomed in.

- Resizing canvas never destroys pixels.

- Builds on Linux and Windows.

- Written in rust.

title.value: Show HN: Paintpot – Kid-friendly MSPaint clone for Linux
